statements.body: The project is for a corner shop that needs a shift handover system for staff.
The handover system must capture till discrepancies at shift end.
The handover system must capture deliveries that arrived during a shift.
The handover system must capture items that need to be reordered.
Staff currently fail to fill in a paper handover notebook reliably, which is the core problem to solve.
How many staff members will use the system, and across how many shifts per day?
What device or platform will staff use to fill in handover records (shared tablet, personal phones, desktop)?
Sensitive credentials mentioned in the idea (till code and alarm word) will not be stored, displayed, or referenced by the system; their handling is a safety concern to resolve with the owner.
Who is the owner or manager who reviews handover records, and do they need a separate view or role?
Whether the system needs authentication or access control for different staff roles is not yet decided.

concerns.coverage: Staff do not reliably complete shift handover records; till discrepancies, deliveries, and reorder needs go unrecorded or uncommunicated between shifts.
Corner shop staff are the primary operators filling in records; a manager or owner likely reviews them, but their role and count are not yet stated.
Work enters at shift start or during a shift (deliveries, till events, stock needs) and must be recorded so the incoming shift can act on it; exact handoff steps and review path are not yet defined.
The system will hold till discrepancy records, delivery logs, and reorder lists per shift; volume, retention period, and export needs are not yet stated.

The idea asked for live display of a till PIN and an alarm code; these must not be stored or displayed by the system — this is an unresolved credential-exposure risk that the owner must decide how to handle outside this tool.

candidates.body: What observable change would tell you the tool is working — for example, a target like every shift having a completed handover record within its first month of use?
candidates.whySelected: Success is the only uncovered core concern; without observable evidence of success, there is no way to judge whether the tool beat the paper notebook it replaces.

candidates.body: Why do staff currently skip the paper notebook — is it time pressure at shift change, unclear expectations, or something else?
candidates.whySelected: The core problem is non-compliance with the existing notebook; understanding the cause of that failure determines whether a digital tool will fare any better and shapes what the first slice must make easy.

candidates.body: How long must handover records be kept, and does anyone ever need to look back more than a few shifts (for example to trace a recurring till discrepancy)?
candidates.whySelected: Retention is an open gap in data coverage and bounds whether the first slice needs history and search or only the latest handover.

readyAdvice.why: Success remains uncovered, and open unknowns about staff count, device platform, and the reviewer role mean the first vertical slice is not yet bounded. Answering the success question and at least one of the existing device/user unknowns would bring the seed close to sufficient.

statements.body: Shift handovers currently happen verbally (word of mouth) rather than in writing, so there is no recorded trail.
Till discrepancies are typically discovered days after they occur, not at the time of the relevant shift.
When a discrepancy surfaces, it cannot be attributed to a specific shift or staff member because no contemporaneous record exists.
The absence of a written record — not staff unwillingness — is the primary reason discrepancies go unresolved; a simple, low-friction recording step at shift end would change the outcome.

concerns.coverage: The real failure mode is verbal-only handover: issues surface days late with no shift-level attribution, making accountability and correction impossible.
With no written record, disputed discrepancies cannot be traced to a shift or individual, creating financial accountability risk for both staff and the owner.
A leading success indicator can now be stated: discrepancies are recorded at the shift they occur and are attributable to a specific shift, reducing the lag from days to same-day.

candidates.body: Should each handover entry identify the specific staff member who recorded it, and if so, how will staff identify themselves at entry time (for example, tapping their name from a list versus logging in with credentials)?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger's success criterion depends on attributing discrepancies to a shift and person, but authentication is undecided and the problem framing demands a low-friction recording step. Resolving how attribution happens directly settles that tension and determines the core data model and entry flow for the first slice.

candidates.body: What device will staff use to fill in handover records at shift end — a shared device at the counter, their personal phones, or an existing shop computer?
candidates.whySelected: This is an already-approved open unknown, and the answer bounds nearly every implementation choice for the first slice: form factor, whether identification can be implicit (shared device needs explicit picker), and whether offline entry matters in a small shop.

candidates.body: What exactly must a staff member fill in at shift end for the entry to count as a complete handover — is it three fixed fields (till discrepancy, deliveries, reorders), or can any of them be skipped when there is nothing to report?
candidates.whySelected: The slice hinges on the minimal record shape. Knowing which fields are mandatory versus skippable defines the low-friction entry form the problem statement says is the fix, and lets a first version ship without guessing at the schema.

candidates.body: How many staff work at the shop, and how many shift changes happen per day?
candidates.whySelected: An already-approved unknown; the answer sizes the identification mechanism (a name picker works for five staff, not fifty) and the daily record volume, but it constrains the slice less than the attribution and device questions.

contradictions.summary: The ledger states that discrepancies must become attributable to a specific shift and staff member, and that the fix is a low-friction recording step — yet whether the system has any authentication or identity mechanism is explicitly undecided. Per-person attribution requires some form of identification, which risks adding exactly the friction the problem framing says must be avoided.

readyAdvice.why: The problem, users, and success criteria are well established, but the first slice cannot be bounded until the attribution/identification approach and the entry device are decided — both shape the entry flow, the data model, and whether the promised low-friction property holds. One or two more answered questions should make the seed slice-ready.

statements.body: There are six part-time staff members who will use the system.
Staff will enter handover records on a single shared shop tablet.
The owner reviews handover records remotely from home, not on the shop tablet.
The owner reviews records on a weekly cadence, not in real time.

A lightweight staff-identification method (e.g. tapping a name from a list) is likely sufficient given a shared tablet with no per-user login currently planned, but this should be confirmed before building authentication.
How the owner accesses records remotely — whether via a web view, exported report, or other mechanism — is not yet stated.

concerns.coverage: Six part-time staff operate the shared shop tablet; the owner is the sole reviewer, accessing records remotely from home on a weekly basis.

Staff record handover items on a shared tablet at the shop; the owner reviews those records remotely from home, suggesting the system needs a remote-accessible read path separate from the tablet entry point.

The system must remain usable on a single shared shop tablet with no indication of dedicated IT support; remote access for the owner implies a hosted or web-accessible component rather than a purely local solution.
Single shared tablet as the staff-side hardware is a confirmed constraint; remote home access for the owner implies the solution cannot be purely offline or local-only.

candidates.body: How should the owner access handover records from home — a simple web page they can log into, an emailed weekly summary, or some other mechanism?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger explicitly marks the owner's remote access path as unstated (statement 0d3c8818), yet it is the single biggest architectural fork: a web view implies a hosted service with access control, while an emailed digest could keep the tablet-side app nearly local. Answering it bounds the first vertical slice more than any other open item.

candidates.body: How long do handover records need to be kept, and does the owner ever need to export them (for example, for accounting or a discrepancy dispute)?
candidates.whySelected: Data coverage notes retention and export are unstated. Since a stated goal is attributing discrepancies to shifts after the fact, retention directly affects whether the tool delivers its accountability value, and export needs shape the owner-side read path.

candidates.body: Is there anything this tool should deliberately not do in its first version — for example, stock management, rota scheduling, or till integration?
candidates.whySelected: Non-goals coverage exists only implicitly; naming explicit exclusions now prevents the shift-handover notebook from silently growing into a shop-management system, which is the classic scope failure for small-business tools.

candidates.body: At shift end, how much time can staff realistically spend on the handover entry before they skip it — under a minute, a couple of minutes, or longer?
candidates.whySelected: The ledger's core hypothesis (fce33b38) is that a low-friction recording step changes staff behavior. Quantifying the friction budget makes that hypothesis testable and directly constrains the entry-form design of the first slice.

readyAdvice.why: All core concerns have some coverage and the problem, users, and constraints are well established, but the owner's remote access mechanism — an explicitly recorded unknown — determines whether the first slice needs a hosted component. That single answer, plus retention expectations, would make the seed sufficient to start building.
